title: A Five Alarm Fire at the White House
text:
A Five Alarm Fire at the White House
It's hard to describe what a disaster this was
When I read the description from Shane Almgren (of The Trumpland Diary Substack) of what happened at the White House yesterday, I couldn’t believe it. Not because Shane isn’t credible—he sure is—but because of the staggering implications.
This was a fire-everybody, convene a secret meeting, and talk 25th Amendment level moment.
Let me give you a critical excerpt from Shane (lightly edited for length):
The Melon Felon hosted the CEOs of most of the oil industry at the White House today in what was one of most bizarre meetings you’ll ever see…trying to convince these oil big wigs to invest some money into Venezuela since he just assured Hannity last night they'd already pledged $100 billion.
At one point—in the middle of HIS OWN speech —Trump just got up from the table and wandered over to look out the window while Rubio and Vance stare at each other and raised their eyes in alarm…
Not only did he get no commitments from ANY company in the room, Exxon CEO Darren Woods told Trump to his face that Venezuela in “uninvestable.”
It’s such a colorful description that it seems exaggerated for effect…but it isn’t. For the record, this gibes exactly with the description in the New York Times1: a brutally awkward scene where top executives tell Trump in no uncertain terms that his publicly-announced fantasies are insane,2 and he wanders around and makes bizarre, rambling suggestions of the inject-your-self-with-disinfectant ilk.3
But then I realized that I didn’t need to trust Shane, or the NYT, or anyone else, because the White House televised this live.
For example, here’s that unbelievably disturbing moment where Trump wanders off to the window [note: I posted this on the Worth Knowing YouTube channel—so while you’re checking this out PLEASE hit Subscribe over there…it helps!]. This 90 seconds is worth watching. Check out especially the moment at the 21-second mark where Secretary of State Marco Rubio looks across at Vice-President JD Vance and raises his eyebrows in…resignation, alarm, dismay, dread? It’s hard to know, but it sure wasn’t good.
There are three inescapable conclusions from this entire episode, in ascending order of urgency and importance:
Firings In any other presidential administration in history, there would be immediate firings across the White House for something like this. Like, a complete house-cleaning. As a congressional chief of staff, I once had my boss give a single, loose quote to a reporter. We were in a tight re-election race, and couldn’t afford mistakes or bad headlines. I got an instant, angry call from the Democratic leadership demanding to know how we, as staff, had screwed this up so badly, because it was our responsibility to get him prepared and make this go well.
That was for a single quote to a reporter. This was a pre-planned White House meeting with some of the richest, most powerful people on earth, to discuss something that the President of the United States had already committed to and apparently gone to war for, that the White House deliberately televised live.
In any other administration, this meeting would have been the subject of weeks of planning, behind the scenes negotiation, and assurances about what exactly the executives would commit to. Any subsequent failure like the catastrophic rejection on camera that Trump was just subjected to would have been an administration-shaping moment, and the only cure, the only way to save the presidency, would have been to scapegoat the staff and make heads roll. No sign of that here, because they are past the point of trying to clean up disasters, and the media has been so inured to them that this didn’t even lead the Times.
Impeachment Think about the implications here. The President of the United States instituted a military operation in clear violation of international law, and then explained in no uncertain terms that the supposed justification—law enforcement for drug crimes—was meaningless, and that the real reason for doing this was to secure a position for oil companies. That alone is potentially impeachable.
Except the oil angle just turned out to be a fraud too.
It’s hard to decide what’s worse: going to war on a flimsy, illegal justification, or going to war with no plan at all. Because that’s what this White House meeting revealed. There was no plan. But either way, this is such an incredible failure of judgement that it can and should lead to an immediate impeachment inquiry.
25th Amendment President Joe Biden once had an embarrassing moment where he didn’t know how to exit a studio, so he wandered off in front of the camera. Republicans screamed “dementia” for weeks and weeks. And clearly, they weren’t totally off-base: Biden’s cognitive faculties were no longer as sharp as they once were by the end of his presidency.
This was President Trump rambling incoherently, riffing off the cuff, and wandering away from a high-stakes meeting with hundreds of billions of dollars and the fate of nations at stake which was supposed to justify his legally dicey attack and regime change in a foreign nation...to stare out the window and talk about his new ballroom.
Any reasonable person in that cabinet who believes in their oath to uphold the Constitution and who takes their obligation to this nation seriously should be convening a cabinet meeting immediately to talk about removing an obviously incapacitated president before he can do any more hard to himself or this country. This is clear and present danger time.

One exec offered the tiny sliver of a fig leaf of saying well we can send an exploratory team down to Venezuela to check things out, such a light gesture that it only made things more painful.
3
He suggested that $12 billion in claims that ConocoPhillips has been pursuing might make a good write-off. “It’s already been written off,” Ryan Lance, the company’s chief executive, said in response. This is a “duh” level thing that most business executives could have assumed, and that a properly briefed president definitely should have known.
